784	def compute_rollout_correction_and_rejection_mask(
785	    old_log_prob: torch.Tensor,
786	    rollout_log_prob: torch.Tensor,
787	    response_mask: torch.Tensor,
788	    rollout_is: Optional[str] = None,
789	    rollout_is_threshold: Optional[str | float] = 2.0,
790	    rollout_is_batch_normalize: bool = False,
791	    rollout_rs: Optional[str] = None,
792	    rollout_rs_threshold: Optional[str | float] = None,
793	) -> tuple[Optional[DataProto], torch.Tensor, dict[str, float]]:
794	    """Unified interface for computing IS weights and rejection masks.
795	
796	    This function combines IS weight calculation (truncated) and rejection sampling (masked)
797	    into a single pipeline.
798	
799	    Key design:
800	    - Separation of IS weights (for variance reduction) and rejection masks (for sample filtering)
801	    - Comprehensive metrics tracking for mismatch diagnosis
802	
803	    Args:
804	        old_log_prob: Log probabilities from the training policy (e.g., FSDP FP32),
805	            shape (batch_size, seq_length).
806	        rollout_log_prob: Log probabilities from the rollout policy (e.g., vLLM BF16),
807	            shape (batch_size, seq_length).
808	        response_mask: Binary mask for valid tokens (1=valid, 0=padding),
809	            shape (batch_size, seq_length).
810	        rollout_is: IS weight aggregation level (see compute_rollout_correction_weights for options).
811	            Set to None to disable IS weight computation.
812	        rollout_is_threshold: Threshold specification for IS weights.
813	            Single float implies TIS; "lower_upper" implies IcePop.
814	        rollout_rs: Rejection sampling aggregation modes as a comma separated string
815	            (see compute_rollout_rejection_mask for the full list). Set to None to disable
816	            rejection sampling.
817	        rollout_rs_threshold: Threshold specification string (see compute_rollout_rejection_mask for details).
818	            Provide one threshold per option (comma separated). For K1-style options, specify
819	            ``lower_upper`` to denote the lower/upper ratio bounds.
820	        rollout_is_batch_normalize: Whether to normalize IS weights to have mean=1.0 per batch.
821	            Default: False.
822	
823	    Returns:
824	        Tuple containing:
825	            rollout_is_weights_proto: DataProto with IS weights (None if rollout_is is None),
826	                key "rollout_is_weights", shape (batch_size, seq_length).
827	            modified_response_mask: Response mask with rejection sampling applied,
828	                shape (batch_size, seq_length).
829	            metrics: Dictionary of all metrics (prefixed with "rollout_corr/"), including:
830	                - IS weight statistics
831	                - Rejection sampling rates
832	                - Policy mismatch metrics (KL, PPL, etc.)
833	    """
834	    # Validate input masks
835	    if not response_mask.any():
836	        raise ValueError("response_mask must contain at least one valid token (1).")
837	    if old_log_prob.shape != rollout_log_prob.shape:
838	        raise ValueError(
839	            f"old_log_prob shape {old_log_prob.shape} does not match rollout_log_prob shape {rollout_log_prob.shape}."
840	        )
841	    if old_log_prob.shape != response_mask.shape:
842	        raise ValueError(
843	            f"log_prob shape {old_log_prob.shape} does not match response_mask shape {response_mask.shape}."
844	        )
845	
846	    # Step 1: Compute log ratio (log(π_train / π_rollout))
847	    log_ratio: torch.Tensor = old_log_prob - rollout_log_prob
848	    metrics: dict[str, float] = {}
849	
850	    # Step 2: Compute IS weights (if enabled)
851	    rollout_is_weights: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None
852	    if rollout_is is not None and rollout_is_threshold is not None:
853	        rollout_is_weights, is_metrics = compute_rollout_correction_weights(
854	            log_ratio=log_ratio,
855	            response_mask=response_mask,
856	            rollout_is=rollout_is,
857	            rollout_is_threshold=rollout_is_threshold,
858	            rollout_is_batch_normalize=rollout_is_batch_normalize,
859	        )
860	        metrics.update(is_metrics)
861	
862	    # Step 3: Compute rejection mask (if enabled)
863	    modified_response_mask: torch.Tensor = response_mask.clone()
864	    if rollout_rs is not None:
865	        if rollout_rs_threshold is None:
866	            raise ValueError(
867	                "rollout_rs_threshold must be explicitly provided when rollout_rs is enabled. "
868	                "Set rollout_rs_threshold to the desired threshold value."
869	            )
870	        modified_response_mask, rs_metrics = compute_rollout_rejection_mask(
871	            log_ratio=log_ratio,
872	            response_mask=response_mask,
873	            rollout_rs=rollout_rs,
874	            rollout_rs_threshold=rollout_rs_threshold,
875	        )
876	        metrics.update(rs_metrics)
877	
878	    # Step 4: Compute off-policy metrics (KL, PPL, χ², etc.)
879	    offpolicy_metrics: dict[str, float] = compute_offpolicy_metrics(
880	        old_log_prob=old_log_prob,
881	        rollout_log_prob=rollout_log_prob,
882	        response_mask=response_mask,
883	    )
884	    metrics.update(offpolicy_metrics)
885	
886	    # Step 6: Add "rollout_corr/" prefix to all metrics for logging consistency
887	    metrics_scalar: dict[str, float] = {}
888	    for key, value in metrics.items():
889	        if isinstance(value, torch.Tensor):
890	            metrics_scalar[f"rollout_corr/{key}"] = value.item()
891	        else:
892	            metrics_scalar[f"rollout_corr/{key}"] = value
893	
894	    # Step 7: Wrap IS weights in DataProto for consistency with API
895	    rollout_is_weights_proto: Optional[DataProto] = None
896	    if rollout_is_weights is not None:
897	        rollout_is_weights_proto = DataProto.from_dict(tensors={"rollout_is_weights": rollout_is_weights})
898	
899	    return rollout_is_weights_proto, modified_response_mask, metrics_scalar

902	def compute_offpolicy_metrics(
903	    old_log_prob: torch.Tensor,
904	    rollout_log_prob: Optional[torch.Tensor],
905	    response_mask: torch.Tensor,
906	) -> dict[str, Any]:
907	    """Compute off-policy diagnostic metrics (helper function).
908	
909	    This helper function operates on raw tensors and is used internally by:
910	    - compute_rollout_correction_and_rejection_mask() in this module (automatically included)
911	    - Tests (test_rollout_corr.py, test_rollout_corr_integration.py)
912	
913	    These metrics help diagnose the off-policy gap between rollout and training policies,
914	    which can arise from:
915	    - Policy mismatch (e.g., vLLM BF16 vs FSDP FP32)
916	    - Model staleness (training on trajectories from older checkpoints)
917	    - General distribution shifts
918	
919	    Key metrics:
920	    - kl: Direct KL divergence estimator KL(π_rollout || π_training)
921	    - k3_kl: K3 KL estimator for stability (more stable for small KL)
922	    - training_ppl: Perplexity of training policy
923	    - rollout_ppl: Perplexity of rollout policy
924	    - log_ppl_diff: Difference in log perplexities
925	    - ppl_ratio: Ratio of training PPL to rollout PPL
926	    - chi2_token: Token-level χ² divergence E[ρ²] - 1
927	    - chi2_seq: Sequence-level χ² divergence E[(∏ρ_t)²] - 1
928	
929	    Args:
930	        old_log_prob: Log probabilities from training policy, shape (batch_size, seq_length)
931	        rollout_log_prob: Log probabilities from rollout policy, shape (batch_size, seq_length)
932	        response_mask: Mask for valid tokens, shape (batch_size, seq_length)
933	
934	    Returns:
935	        Dictionary of off-policy metrics (without prefix)
936	    """
937	    # Validate that we have at least one valid token
938	    assert response_mask.any(), "Expected at least one valid token in response_mask"
939	
940	    metrics = {}
941	
942	    # 1. Training policy perplexity (always available)
943	    # Formula: exp(-1/|T| * Σ log π_training(y_t|y_<t))
944	    # where |T| is the number of tokens generated by the model
945	    mean_log_prob_training = verl_F.masked_mean(old_log_prob, response_mask, axis=-1)  # (batch_size,)
946	    training_ppl = torch.exp(-mean_log_prob_training).mean()  # Batch mean of per-sequence PPL
947	    metrics["training_ppl"] = training_ppl.detach().item()
948	
949	    # Also log log-ppl for easier analysis (avoids exponential scale)
950	    metrics["training_log_ppl"] = (-mean_log_prob_training).mean().detach().item()
951	
952	    # 2. Compute rollout off-policy metrics (only if rollout_log_probs available)
953	    if rollout_log_prob is not None:
954	        # 2a. kl: Direct estimator for KL(π_rollout || π_training)
955	        # This is the standard KL divergence: E[log(π_rollout) - log(π_training)]
956	        # Positive value means rollout policy is more confident than training policy
957	        metrics["kl"] = verl_F.masked_mean(rollout_log_prob - old_log_prob, response_mask).detach().item()
958	
959	        # 2b. k3_kl: K3 estimator for KL(π_rollout || π_training)
960	        # More stable for small KL values using: E[exp(log_ratio) - log_ratio - 1]
961	        # Formula: KL ≈ E[r - log(r) - 1] where r = π_training/π_rollout
962	        log_ratio = old_log_prob - rollout_log_prob
963	        k3_kl_matrix = torch.exp(log_ratio) - log_ratio - 1
964	        metrics["k3_kl"] = verl_F.masked_mean(k3_kl_matrix, response_mask).detach().item()
965	
966	        # 2c. Rollout policy perplexity
967	        mean_log_prob_rollout = verl_F.masked_mean(rollout_log_prob, response_mask, axis=-1)  # (batch_size,)
968	        rollout_ppl = torch.exp(-mean_log_prob_rollout).mean()  # Batch mean of per-sequence PPL
969	        metrics["rollout_ppl"] = rollout_ppl.detach().item()
970	        metrics["rollout_log_ppl"] = (-mean_log_prob_rollout).mean().detach().item()
971	
972	        # 2d. Log PPL difference (sequence-level perplexity difference)
973	        # log_ppl_diff = mean_log_prob_rollout - mean_log_prob_training
974	        # Since ppl = exp(-log_prob), we have:
975	        #   log(ppl_ratio) = log(training_ppl/rollout_ppl) = log_ppl_diff
976	        # Positive value means training assigns lower probability (higher PPL) than rollout
977	        log_ppl_diff = mean_log_prob_rollout - mean_log_prob_training
978	        metrics["log_ppl_diff"] = log_ppl_diff.mean().detach().item()
979	        metrics["log_ppl_abs_diff"] = log_ppl_diff.abs().mean().detach().item()
980	        metrics["log_ppl_diff_max"] = log_ppl_diff.max().detach().item()
981	        metrics["log_ppl_diff_min"] = log_ppl_diff.min().detach().item()
982	
983	        # 2e. PPL ratio (how much higher is training PPL vs rollout PPL)
984	        # Compute per-sequence ratio first, then average
985	        # For numerical stability, compute in log space using log_ppl_diff
986	        # Note: log_ppl_diff = log(ppl_ratio), so ppl_ratio = exp(log_ppl_diff)
987	        # This is the inverse of geometric IS: ppl_ratio_i = 1 / geometric_is_i for each sequence
988	        ppl_ratio = torch.exp(log_ppl_diff).mean()  # mean(exp(log_ppl_diff)) = mean(ppl_ratio_i)
989	        metrics["ppl_ratio"] = ppl_ratio.detach().item()
990	
991	        # 2f. Chi-squared divergence: χ²(π_training || π_rollout) = E_μ[ρ²] - 1
992	        # where ρ = π_training / π_rollout and μ = π_rollout (rollout distribution)
993	        # This measures the variance of importance sampling weights
994	        # Token-level: E_token[ρ²] - 1 (averaged over all tokens)
995	        log_ratio_safe = torch.clamp(log_ratio, min=-SAFETY_BOUND, max=SAFETY_BOUND)
996	        rho_token = torch.exp(log_ratio_safe)  # ρ = π_training / π_rollout (token-level)
997	        rho_squared_token = rho_token.square()
998	        chi2_token = verl_F.masked_mean(rho_squared_token, response_mask) - 1.0
999	        metrics["chi2_token"] = chi2_token.detach().item()
1000	
1001	        # Sequence-level: E_seq[(Π ρ_t)²] - 1 = E_seq[exp(2 * Σ log ρ_t)] - 1
1002	        log_ratio_sum = verl_F.masked_sum(log_ratio, response_mask, axis=-1)  # Σ log ρ_t per sequence
1003	        log_ratio_sum_safe = torch.clamp(log_ratio_sum, min=-SAFETY_BOUND, max=SAFETY_BOUND)
1004	        rho_squared_seq = torch.exp(2.0 * log_ratio_sum_safe)  # (Π ρ_t)²
1005	        chi2_seq = rho_squared_seq.mean() - 1.0
1006	        metrics["chi2_seq"] = chi2_seq.detach().item()
1007	
1008	    return metrics

1011	def compute_rollout_correction_and_add_to_batch(
1012	    batch: DataProto, rollout_corr_config: RolloutCorrectionConfig
1013	) -> tuple[DataProto, dict]:
1014	    """Compute rollout correction weights and apply rejection sampling.
1015	
1016	    Computes importance sampling weights to correct for off-policy issues between
1017	    rollout and training policies. Applies rejection sampling by modifying response_mask.
1018	    Always updates response_mask; conditionally adds IS weights.
1019	
1020	    Key behavior:
1021	    - response_mask: ALWAYS updated with rejection (RS exclusions removed from training)
1022	    - rollout_is_weights: Added to batch ONLY if rollout_is parameter is set
1023	
1024	    This separation ensures:
1025	    - Rejection works independently of IS weight application
1026	    - Metrics can be monitored before enabling IS weight correction
1027

1030

1033	            updated_batch: Batch with modified response_mask (always) and rollout_is_weights (if enabled)
1034	            metrics: Dict of IS and off-policy metrics, all with "rollout_corr/" prefix
1035	
1036	    Note:
1037	        The implementation is copied from szrlee <szrlee@gmail.com>.
1038	    """
1039	    # Get new API parameters directly from config
1040	    rollout_is = rollout_corr_config.get("rollout_is", None)
1041	    rollout_is_threshold = rollout_corr_config.get("rollout_is_threshold", 2.0)
1042	    rollout_is_batch_normalize = rollout_corr_config.get("rollout_is_batch_normalize", False)
1043	    rollout_rs = rollout_corr_config.get("rollout_rs", None)
1044	    rollout_rs_threshold = rollout_corr_config.get("rollout_rs_threshold", None)
1045	
1046	    # Compute IS weights and get modified response_mask
1047	    rollout_is_weights, modified_response_mask, rollout_corr_metrics = compute_rollout_correction_and_rejection_mask(
1048	        old_log_prob=batch.batch["old_log_probs"],
1049	        rollout_log_prob=batch.batch["rollout_log_probs"],
1050	        response_mask=batch.batch["response_mask"],
1051	        rollout_is=rollout_is,
1052	        rollout_is_threshold=rollout_is_threshold,
1053	        rollout_is_batch_normalize=rollout_is_batch_normalize,
1054	        rollout_rs=rollout_rs,
1055	        rollout_rs_threshold=rollout_rs_threshold,
1056	    )
1057	
1058	    # ALWAYS update response_mask with rejection applied
1059	    batch.batch["response_mask"] = modified_response_mask
1060	
1061	    # Add IS weights to batch if computed
1062	    if rollout_is_weights is not None:
1063	        batch = batch.union(rollout_is_weights)
1064	
1065	    return batch, rollout_corr_metrics

Actually wait — the important thing here is that rollout_corr metrics appear in the logs. The run script doesn't set any rollout_corr config explicitly. But the metrics appear... `compute_rollout_corr_metrics_from_logprobs` is called in the actor. Let me check whether that's default-on.

1. The DAPO reward manager + gsm8k reward function.
2. The data preprocessing script (examples/data_preprocess/gsm8k.py).
3. The parquet files.
4. The `training/rollout_probs_diff_*` metrics — computed in the trainer; these compare old_log_probs from actor vs rollout log probs.

Also important: check `critic/score/mean` at 0.58 vs val acc 0.49. And entropy rising 0.27→4.1. That's a big deal.

Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider the entropy. In verl, `actor/entropy` is the mean per-token entropy of the current policy on rollout data. Starting at 0.27 and growing to 4.0 is a massive explosion — the policy is becoming more random over training. For GSM8K GRPO with a 0.5B model at lr 2e-6... entropy rising means the model is flattening its distribution. That is a classic sign of:
- Reward hacking / format gaming with high-temperature sampling
- OR a weight-sync bug where the actor updates drift away from vLLM
- OR the KL/clip not working

But hold on — the val accuracy is stable at ~0.45-0.50 and training reward is ~0.58. If entropy truly exploded, greedy decoding accuracy would degrade. Hmm, entropy 4 nats is very high (uniform over e^4 ≈ 55 tokens). For a 0.5B model with a 150k vocab... per-token entropy of 4 nats means quite diffuse. Actually for a model generating math with high confidence, entropy is more like 0.1-1. So 4 is high but it's the mean over all tokens, including tokens where the model is genuinely uncertain.

Hmm, but note that at step 5 the entropy is 0.27 (very low = confident), then rises steadily. Actually, wait — the entropy at step 5 being 0.27 is remarkably LOW for the base instruct model. Hmm.

Let me consider: is this an entropy explosion caused by a real bug (e.g., weight sync broken so the actor trains on stale data, producing off-policy gradients that flatten the policy)? The `rollout_corr` diagnostics exist to detect exactly that. Let's look at the actual values: `rollout_corr/kl` = E[log π_rollout - log π_train]. Let me extract all the rollout_corr series.

Interesting: `rollout_corr/kl` ≈ 0.18, `ppl_ratio` ≈ 1.13, pearson corr ≈ 0.98-0.99. These are consistent with a moderate degree of rollout/training mismatch, but Pearson 0.98 between actor and rollout probs is basically "fine-ish" (bf16 vs fp32 mismatch typically yields ~0.05 mean abs diff and kl ~0.02-0.05). Here kl=0.185 and probs_diff_mean=0.018. Hmm, that's larger than a pure bf16-vs-fp32 gap but the correlation is 0.99 so the weights are synced correctly (a broken weight sync would give correlation ~0)

The PPL values (945 → 544) are crazy high but that's mean over batch of exp(-mean_log_prob) which is dominated by outliers; not necessarily meaningful.

OK so rollout/training consistency looks acceptable (corr 0.99). Not the smoking gun.

Let's focus. Key observed signals so far:
1. Val acc at step 0 = 0.0008 (essentially 0), then 0.50 at step 10, then flat/declining to 0.43 at step 40, then back to ~0.49. Net: no improvement over the whole run — flat at ~0.48 the whole time. Actually, val at step 10 (0.50) ≈ val at step 100 (0.486). So **zero held-out improvement over 100 steps**, while training score went 0.34 → 0.62.
2. Entropy rises 0.27 → 4.1 — the policy is becoming more random.
3. response_length/clip_ratio rises 0.047 → 0.30, i.e., up to 30% of rollouts hit the 512 token cap.

Hmm wait. Let me reconsider #1. The step-0 val of 0.0008 is an artifact of the base model not using "####" format. At step 10 it's 0.50. So the run "worked" in the sense of teaching format. But then it plateaued and oscillated between 0.43 and 0.50, ending at 0.486 — no net improvement from step 10 to 100. Training reward went from 0.62 at step 10 to 0.58 at step 100 — also basically flat. Actually training score at step 5 is 0.34, step 10 is 0.62, then noisy 0.45-0.65 with no trend.

So the whole run is: format learned in first ~10 steps, then plateau, and ending at ~0.58 train / 0.486 val, with entropy growing.

Is this "healthy"? For a 100-step GRPO run on a 0.5B model, a plateau after format acquisition at ~50% is plausible... Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct GSM8K is around 40-50% typically (model card: 53 for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct... actually Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct GSM8K ≈ 40-50%). So val 48.6% is roughly the base capability. The run didn't really improve held-out accuracy.

But the entropy explosion is the smoking gun for something. Let me examine more carefully. Let me plot all the series at full resolution, and look at additional metrics like `response_length/clip_ratio`, `global_seqlen`, `timing_s`, `gpu_mem.csv`.

Let me also check the diff between train and val prompts: at step 0 val is 0.0008, which means the base model with greedy decoding produced "####" in ~0% of outputs. But during training with temp=1.0/top_p=0.5 at step 5 the score was 0.34. Hmm, that's a huge gap: greedy val gives 0.08% but sampled training gives 34%? At step 5 already. That means even at step ~5 the training rollouts had #### 34% of the time, while the step-0 val had 0.08% of the #### format. Hmm. But step 0 val was BEFORE training. At step 0, training scores are unavailable (step 0 record has None for critic/* in my printout — because step 0 in metrics.jsonl is the val-before-train record). So we don't know the base model training-format rate. Let's check the step-0 val outputs for "####" occurrences.

Actually it's likely the base model almost never emits #### → reward ~0 at step 0 for GRPO too. With GRPO, when all 8 responses in a group get 0, advantage = 0, so no gradient. Format learning would then be impossible unless at least some responses get #### right. With temp=1.0 top_p=0.5 sampling, some small fraction gets the format → GRPO amplifies it → quick jump to 0.5. Yes, that's consistent: greedy base model rarely emits ####; but with sampling at temp 1.0 and 8 tries per prompt there's enough signal to bootstrap.

So the jump 0.0008 → 0.50 is a *format acquisition* artifact, not a capability jump. Fine, that's normal for verl GSM8K GRPO.

So the key question: is the run healthy? Signals to check further:
- Entropy growth 0.27 → 4.1: is this "normal"? In DAPO/GRPO without entropy bonus and with clipping, entropy typically first drops (sharpening) or stays. Growing 15× is a strong sign of policy diffusion toward randomness. Actually hold on, let's be careful: `actor/entropy` in verl is computed with the *sampled* tokens from the rollout. As training progresses and rollouts get dominated by format tokens... no that wouldn't raise entropy.

Actually, in GRPO with group-relative advantages and rule-based binary rewards, when a group is all-correct or all-wrong, advantage is 0. As accuracy rises toward ~0.6, more groups become all-correct → no gradient. The gradient signal concentrates on borderline prompts. Combined with token-mean loss aggregation... hmm.

"""
Preprocess the GSM8k dataset to parquet format
"""

import argparse
import os
import re

import datasets

from verl.utils.hdfs_io import copy, makedirs


def extract_solution(solution_str):
    solution = re.search("#### (\\-?[0-9\\.\\,]+)", solution_str)
    assert solution is not None
    final_solution = solution.group(0)
    final_solution = final_solution.split("#### ")[1].replace(",", "")
    return final_solution


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--local_dir", default=None, help="The save directory for the preprocessed dataset.")
    parser.add_argument("--hdfs_dir", default=None)
    parser.add_argument("--local_dataset_path", default=None, help="The local path to the raw dataset, if it exists.")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--local_save_dir", default="~/data/gsm8k", help="The save directory for the preprocessed dataset."
    )

    args = parser.parse_args()
    local_dataset_path = args.local_dataset_path

    data_source = "openai/gsm8k"

    if local_dataset_path is not None:
        dataset = datasets.load_dataset(local_dataset_path, "main")
    else:
        dataset = datasets.load_dataset(data_source, "main")

    train_dataset = dataset["train"]
    test_dataset = dataset["test"]

    instruction_following = 'Let\'s think step by step and output the final answer after "####".'

    # add a row to each data item that represents a unique id
    def make_map_fn(split):
        def process_fn(example, idx):
            question_raw = example.pop("question")

            question = question_raw + " " + instruction_following

            answer_raw = example.pop("answer")
            solution = extract_solution(answer_raw)
            data = {
                "data_source": data_source,
                "prompt": [
                    {
                        "role": "user",
                        "content": question,
                    }
                ],
                "ability": "math",
                "reward_model": {"style": "rule", "ground_truth": solution},
                "extra_info": {
                    "split": split,
                    "index": idx,
                    "answer": answer_raw,
                    "question": question_raw,
                },
            }
            return data

        return process_fn

    train_dataset = train_dataset.map(function=make_map_fn("train"), with_indices=True)
    test_dataset = test_dataset.map(function=make_map_fn("test"), with_indices=True)

    hdfs_dir = args.hdfs_dir
    local_save_dir = args.local_dir
    if local_save_dir is not None:
        print("Warning: Argument 'local_dir' is deprecated. Please use 'local_save_dir' instead.")
    else:
        local_save_dir = args.local_save_dir

    train_dataset.to_parquet(os.path.join(local_save_dir, "train.parquet"))
    test_dataset.to_parquet(os.path.join(local_save_dir, "test.parquet"))

    if hdfs_dir is not None:
        makedirs(hdfs_dir)

        copy(src=local_save_dir, dst=hdfs_dir)

import re

_SOLUTION_CLIP_CHARS = 300


def extract_solution(solution_str, method="strict"):
    assert method in ["strict", "flexible"]

    # Optimization: Regular expression matching on very long strings can be slow.
    # For math problems, the final answer is usually at the end.
    # We only match on the last 300 characters, which is a safe approximation for 300 tokens.
    if len(solution_str) > _SOLUTION_CLIP_CHARS:
        solution_str = solution_str[-_SOLUTION_CLIP_CHARS:]

    if method == "strict":
        # this also tests the formatting of the model
        solutions = re.findall("#### (\\-?[0-9\\.\\,]+)", solution_str)
        if len(solutions) == 0:
            final_answer = None
        else:
            # take the last solution
            final_answer = solutions[-1].replace(",", "").replace("$", "")
    elif method == "flexible":
        answer = re.findall("(\\-?[0-9\\.\\,]+)", solution_str)
        final_answer = None
        if len(answer) == 0:
            # no reward is there is no answer
            pass
        else:
            invalid_str = ["", "."]
            # find the last number that is not '.'
            for final_answer in reversed(answer):
                if final_answer not in invalid_str:
                    break
    return final_answer


def compute_score(solution_str, ground_truth, method="strict", format_score=0.0, score=1.0):
    """The scoring function for GSM8k.

    Reference: Trung, Luong, et al. "Reft: Reasoning with reinforced fine-tuning." Proceedings of the 62nd Annual
    Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

    Args:
        solution_str: the solution text
        ground_truth: the ground truth
        method: the method to extract the solution, choices are 'strict' and 'flexible'
        format_score: the score for the format
        score: the score for the correct answer
    """
    answer = extract_solution(solution_str=solution_str, method=method)
    if answer is None:
        return 0
    else:
        if answer == ground_truth:
            return score
        else:
            return format_score

from verl.workers.reward_manager.abstract import AbstractRewardManager


@register("dapo")
class DAPORewardManager(AbstractRewardManager):
    """The reward manager."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        tokenizer,
        num_examine,
        compute_score=None,
        reward_fn_key="data_source",
        max_resp_len=None,
        overlong_buffer_cfg=None,
    ) -> None:
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.num_examine = num_examine  # the number of batches of decoded responses to print to the console
        self.compute_score = compute_score or default_compute_score
        self.reward_fn_key = reward_fn_key
        self.overlong_buffer_cfg = overlong_buffer_cfg
        self.max_resp_len = max_resp_len

        if self.overlong_buffer_cfg is not None and self.overlong_buffer_cfg.enable:
            assert self.max_resp_len is not None, (
                f"max_resp_len must be provided if {overlong_buffer_cfg=}, but got None"
            )
            assert self.max_resp_len >= self.overlong_buffer_cfg.len, (
                "max_resp_len must be larger than overlong_buffer.len"
            )
            assert self.overlong_buffer_cfg.len > 0, (
                "overlong_buffer.len must be positive when overlong penalty is enabled,"
                f"but got {self.overlong_buffer_cfg.len}."
                "To disable the overlong penalty, set overlong_buffer.enable = False"
            )

    def __call__(self, data: DataProto, return_dict: bool = False):
        """We will expand this function gradually based on the available datasets"""

        # If there is rm score, we directly return rm score. Otherwise, we compute via rm_score_fn
        reward_from_rm_scores = self._extract_reward_from_rm_scores(data, return_dict)
        if reward_from_rm_scores is not None:
            return reward_from_rm_scores

        reward_tensor = torch.zeros_like(data.batch["responses"], dtype=torch.float32)
        reward_extra_info = defaultdict(list)

        already_print_data_sources = {}

        for i in range(len(data)):
            data_item = data[i]  # DataProtoItem

            prompt_ids = data_item.batch["prompts"]

            prompt_length = prompt_ids.shape[-1]

            valid_prompt_length = data_item.batch["attention_mask"][:prompt_length].sum()
            valid_prompt_ids = prompt_ids[-valid_prompt_length:]

            response_ids = data_item.batch["responses"]
            valid_response_length = data_item.batch["attention_mask"][prompt_length:].sum()
            valid_response_ids = response_ids[:valid_response_length]

            # decode
            prompt_str = self.tokenizer.decode(valid_prompt_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
            response_str = self.tokenizer.decode(valid_response_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
            eos_token = self.tokenizer.eos_token
            if response_str.endswith(eos_token):
                response_str = response_str[: -len(eos_token)]

            ground_truth = data_item.non_tensor_batch["reward_model"]["ground_truth"]

            data_source = data_item.non_tensor_batch[self.reward_fn_key]

            extra_info = data_item.non_tensor_batch.get("extra_info", {})

            rollout_reward_scores = data_item.non_tensor_batch.get("reward_scores", {})

            extra_info["rollout_reward_scores"] = rollout_reward_scores

            result = self.compute_score(
                data_source=data_source,
                solution_str=response_str,
                ground_truth=ground_truth,
                extra_info=extra_info,
            )

            score: float
            if isinstance(result, dict):
                score = result["score"]
                # Store the information including original reward
                for key, value in result.items():
                    reward_extra_info[key].append(value)
            else:
                score = result
                reward_extra_info["acc"].append(score)

            reward = score

            if self.overlong_buffer_cfg is not None and self.overlong_buffer_cfg.enable:
                overlong_buffer_len = self.overlong_buffer_cfg.len
                expected_len = self.max_resp_len - overlong_buffer_len
                exceed_len = valid_response_length - expected_len
                overlong_penalty_factor = self.overlong_buffer_cfg.penalty_factor
                overlong_reward = min(-exceed_len / overlong_buffer_len * overlong_penalty_factor, 0)
                reward += overlong_reward
                if self.overlong_buffer_cfg.log:
                    reward_extra_info["overlong_reward"].append(overlong_reward)
                    reward_extra_info["overlong"].append(overlong_reward < 0)

            reward_tensor[i, valid_response_length - 1] = reward

            if data_source not in already_print_data_sources:
                already_print_data_sources[data_source] = 0

            if already_print_data_sources[data_source] < self.num_examine:
                already_print_data_sources[data_source] += 1
                print("[prompt]", prompt_str)
                print("[response]", response_str)
                print("[ground_truth]", ground_truth)
                if isinstance(result, dict):
                    for key, value in result.items():
                        print(f"[{key}]", value)
                else:
                    print("[score]", score)

        if return_dict:
            return {
                "reward_tensor": reward_tensor,
                "reward_extra_info": reward_extra_info,
            }
        else:
            return reward_tensor

def default_compute_score(
    data_source,
    solution_str,
    ground_truth,
    extra_info=None,
    sandbox_fusion_url=None,
    concurrent_semaphore=None,
    memory_limit_mb=None,
    **kwargs,
):
    """Compute the score for a given solution based on the data source.

    Args:
        data_source (str): The source dataset identifier which determines the scoring method.
        solution_str (str): The solution string to be evaluated.
        ground_truth (str): The ground truth answer for comparison.
        extra_info (dict, optional): Additional information that might be needed for scoring. Defaults to None.

    Returns:
        float: The computed score as a floating point number. If the result is a dictionary,
               it returns the dictionary instead.

    Raises:
        NotImplementedError: If the reward function is not implemented for the given data source.
    """

        advantages (torch.Tensor):
            Advantage estimates for each action, shape (batch_size, response_length).
        response_mask (torch.Tensor):
            Mask indicating which tokens to include in the loss, shape (batch_size, response_length).
        cliprange (float, optional):

            Defaults to None (must be provided).
        cliprange_low (float, optional):
            Lower clip range for dual-clip PPO. Defaults to same as `cliprange`.
        cliprange_high (float, optional):
            Upper clip range for dual-clip PPO. Defaults to same as `cliprange`.
        clip_ratio_c (float, optional):
            Lower bound of the ratio for dual-clip PPO. See https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.09729.

    negative_approx_kl = torch.clamp(negative_approx_kl, min=-20.0, max=20.0)

def compute_grpo_outcome_advantage(
    token_level_rewards: torch.Tensor,
    response_mask: torch.Tensor,
    index: np.ndarray,
    epsilon: float = 1e-6,
    norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo: bool = True,
    config: Optional[AlgoConfig] = None,
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    """
    Compute advantage for GRPO, operating only on Outcome reward
    (with only one scalar reward for each response).

    Args:
        token_level_rewards: `(torch.Tensor)`
            shape is (bs, response_length)
        response_mask: `(torch.Tensor)`
            shape is (bs, response_length)
        index: `(np.ndarray)`
            index array for grouping
        epsilon: `(float)`
            small value to avoid division by zero
        norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo: `(bool)`
            whether to scale the GRPO advantage
        config: `(Optional[AlgoConfig])`
            algorithm configuration object

    Note:
        If norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo is True, the advantage is scaled by the std, as in the original GRPO.
        If False, the advantage is not scaled, as in Dr.GRPO (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783).

    Returns:
        advantages: `(torch.Tensor)`
            shape is (bs, response_length)
        Returns: `(torch.Tensor)`
            shape is (bs, response_length)
    """
    scores = token_level_rewards.sum(dim=-1)

    id2score = defaultdict(list)
    id2mean = {}
    id2std = {}

    with torch.no_grad():
        bsz = scores.shape[0]
        for i in range(bsz):
            id2score[index[i]].append(scores[i])
        for idx in id2score:
            if len(id2score[idx]) == 1:
                id2mean[idx] = torch.tensor(0.0)
                id2std[idx] = torch.tensor(1.0)
            elif len(id2score[idx]) > 1:
                scores_tensor = torch.stack(id2score[idx])
                id2mean[idx] = torch.mean(scores_tensor)
                id2std[idx] = torch.std(scores_tensor)
            else:
                raise ValueError(f"no score in prompt index: {idx}")
        for i in range(bsz):
            if norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo:
                scores[i] = (scores[i] - id2mean[index[i]]) / (id2std[index[i]] + epsilon)
            else:
                scores[i] = scores[i] - id2mean[index[i]]
        scores = scores.unsqueeze(-1) * response_mask

    return scores, scores

def compute_grpo_vectorized_outcome_advantage(
    token_level_rewards: torch.Tensor,
    response_mask: torch.Tensor,

    config: Optional[AlgoConfig] = None,

    """

      a_i = \\frac{r_i - \\mu_g}{\\sigma_g} (or without dividing by \\sigma_g),

        if norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo:
            scalars = (scores - mean_g[g]) / (std_g[g] + epsilon)
        else:
            scalars = scores - mean_g[g]
        advantages = scalars.unsqueeze(-1) * response_mask
        return advantages, advantages

import logging

import torch

from verl.protocol import DataProto

logger = logging.getLogger(__file__)


def calculate_token_list_diff(tensor1: torch.Tensor, tensor2: torch.Tensor, mask: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    # verify inputs
    if tensor1.numel() == 0 or tensor2.numel() == 0:
        return torch.zeros(tensor1.shape[0], dtype=torch.long, device=tensor1.device)
    if tensor1.shape != tensor2.shape or mask.shape != tensor1.shape or mask.shape != tensor2.shape:
        print(
            f"<WARN> dim of tensor1, tensor2, mask is not equal, {(tensor1.shape)=},{(tensor2.shape)=}, {(mask.shape)=}"
        )
        return torch.ones_like(tensor1)
    # transfer to same device
    if tensor2.device != tensor1.device:
        tensor2 = tensor2.to(tensor1.device)
    if mask.device != tensor1.device:
        mask = mask.to(tensor1.device)

    # calculate diff
    diff_mask = tensor1 != tensor2

    valid_diff_mask = diff_mask & (mask == 1)

    diff_counts = valid_diff_mask.sum(dim=1)

    return diff_counts


def pearson_correlation_coefficient(tensor1: torch.Tensor, tensor2: torch.Tensor, mask: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    # implemention of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.13585
    if tensor1.shape != tensor2.shape or mask.shape != tensor1.shape or mask.shape != tensor2.shape:
        return 0
    mt1 = torch.masked_select(tensor1, mask)
    mt2 = torch.masked_select(tensor2, mask)
    result = torch.corrcoef(torch.stack([mt1, mt2], dim=0))
    return result[0][1].detach().item()


def calculate_log_prob_diff(log_probs1: torch.Tensor, log_probs2: torch.Tensor, mask: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    full_diff = torch.abs(log_probs1 - log_probs2)
    return torch.masked_select(full_diff, mask)


def calculate_debug_metrics(data: DataProto) -> dict:
    """
    calculate rollout vs actor logprobs diff, for debugging purpose

    Args:
        data: DataProto
            the data batch to calculate
            rollout_log_probs: log_probs record when rollout forward tokens

def entropy_from_logits(logits: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Calculate Shannon entropy from unnormalized logits.

    Computes H(p) = -sum(p * log(p)) using the numerically stable formula:
    entropy = logsumexp(logits) - sum(softmax(logits) * logits)

    Args:
        logits: Unnormalized log-probabilities of shape (..., vocab_size).

    Returns:
        torch.Tensor: Entropy values with shape (...,), one per distribution.
    """
    pd = torch.nn.functional.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
    entropy = torch.logsumexp(logits, dim=-1) - torch.sum(pd * logits, dim=-1)
    return entropy

def compute_policy_loss_vanilla(
    old_log_prob: torch.Tensor,
    log_prob: torch.Tensor,
    advantages: torch.Tensor,
    response_mask: torch.Tensor,
    loss_agg_mode: str = "token-mean",
    config: Optional[ActorConfig] = None,
    rollout_is_weights: torch.Tensor | None = None,
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Compute the clipped policy objective and related metrics for PPO.

    Adapted from
    https://github.com/huggingface/trl/blob/main/trl/trainer/ppo_trainer.py#L1122

    Args:
        old_log_prob (torch.Tensor):
            Log-probabilities of actions under the old policy, shape (batch_size, response_length).
        log_prob (torch.Tensor):
            Log-probabilities of actions under the current policy, shape (batch_size, response_length).
        advantages (torch.Tensor):
            Advantage estimates for each action, shape (batch_size, response_length).
        response_mask (torch.Tensor):
            Mask indicating which tokens to include in the loss, shape (batch_size, response_length).
        loss_agg_mode (str, optional):
            Aggregation mode for `agg_loss`. Defaults to "token-mean".
        config: `(verl.trainer.config.ActorConfig)`:
            config for the actor.
        rollout_log_probs: `(torch.Tensor)`:
            log probabilities of actions under the rollout policy, shape (batch_size, response_length).
    """

    assert config is not None
    assert not isinstance(config, AlgoConfig)
    clip_ratio = config.clip_ratio  # Clipping parameter ε for standard PPO. See https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347.
    clip_ratio_low = config.clip_ratio_low if config.clip_ratio_low is not None else clip_ratio
    clip_ratio_high = config.clip_ratio_high if config.clip_ratio_high is not None else clip_ratio
    clip_ratio_c = config.get(  # Lower bound of the ratio for dual-clip PPO. See https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.09729.
        "clip_ratio_c", 3.0
    )

    cliprange = clip_ratio
    cliprange_low = clip_ratio_low
    cliprange_high = clip_ratio_high

    assert clip_ratio_c > 1.0, (
        "The lower bound of the clip_ratio_c for dual-clip PPO should be greater than 1.0,"
        + f" but get the value: {clip_ratio_c}."
    )

    negative_approx_kl = log_prob - old_log_prob
    # Clamp negative_approx_kl for stability
    negative_approx_kl = torch.clamp(negative_approx_kl, min=-20.0, max=20.0)
    ratio = torch.exp(negative_approx_kl)
    ppo_kl = verl_F.masked_mean(-negative_approx_kl, response_mask)

    pg_losses1 = -advantages * ratio
    if cliprange_low is None:
        cliprange_low = cliprange
    if cliprange_high is None:
        cliprange_high = cliprange
    pg_losses2 = -advantages * torch.clamp(
        ratio, 1 - cliprange_low, 1 + cliprange_high
    )  # - clip(ratio, 1-cliprange, 1+cliprange) * A
    clip_pg_losses1 = torch.maximum(
        pg_losses1, pg_losses2
    )  # max(-ratio * A, -clip(ratio, 1-cliprange, 1+cliprange) * A)
    pg_clipfrac = verl_F.masked_mean(torch.gt(pg_losses2, pg_losses1).float(), response_mask)

    pg_losses3 = -advantages * clip_ratio_c
    clip_pg_losses2 = torch.min(pg_losses3, clip_pg_losses1)
    pg_clipfrac_lower = verl_F.masked_mean(
        torch.gt(clip_pg_losses1, pg_losses3) * (advantages < 0).float(), response_mask
    )

    pg_losses = torch.where(advantages < 0, clip_pg_losses2, clip_pg_losses1)

    # Apply rollout correction weights if provided
    if rollout_is_weights is not None:
        pg_losses = pg_losses * rollout_is_weights

    pg_loss = agg_loss(
        loss_mat=pg_losses, loss_mask=response_mask, loss_agg_mode=loss_agg_mode, **config.global_batch_info
    )

    pg_metrics = {
        "actor/pg_clipfrac": pg_clipfrac.detach().item(),
        "actor/ppo_kl": ppo_kl.detach().item(),
        "actor/pg_clipfrac_lower": pg_clipfrac_lower.detach().item(),
    }
    return pg_loss, pg_metrics

Let me continue the verification work. I have a few remaining items:

1. Confirm `norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo` default in `verl/trainer/config/algorithm.py` and that `rollout_correction` is unset.
2. Check `ppo_mini_batch_size` semantics in the FSDP actor — whether 32 sequences → 4 optimizer steps (1024/32=32? or 32 prompts?). Actually the script comment says "4 optimizer steps per training step" with PPO_MINI_BATCH_SIZE=32 and TRAIN_BATCH_SIZE=128. So 128/32 = 4 — mini-batches are counted in prompts, and each prompt group of 8 rollouts stays together. Let me verify this in the engine worker code.
3. Verify entropy gradient direction: with entropy_coeff=0, the entropy increase is not explicitly maximized; it's an emergent effect of the policy loss. The mechanism: token-mean loss normalization + group-relative advantages where truncated long responses get A<0. Actually let me think about the mechanism more carefully.

Actually, let me think about the established facts and what remains uncertain:

**Established:**
- Held-out acc: 0.0008 (step 0) → 0.5004 (step 10) → ~0.48-0.50 through step 100 (0.4860 final). No held-out improvement after step 10.
- actor/entropy: 0.2636 → 2.248 (step 17) → 5.061 (step 63) → 2.86 (step 100). Massive flattening.
- response_length/clip_ratio: 0.04 → peak 0.3672 (step 63) → ~0.18-0.31 late. Truncation at 512 tokens.
- rollout_log_ppl: 0.037 → 1.31. Model's own samples become unlikely under itself.
- actor/kl_loss: rising to ~0.4-0.5.
- Training reward plateaus ~0.58.
- All truncated responses score 0 (never emit "####").
- Runtime clean; no OOM; weight sync fine (pearson 0.986).
- Reward logic correct; data clean; no leakage.
- top_p=0.5 renormalization artifacts (rollout_corr/kl +0.185, ppl_ratio 1.13, negative chi2_token) — red herring, not a bug.

**Root cause hypothesis:** GRPO misconfiguration causing entropy explosion + truncation feedback loop. Key elements:
1. `norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo=True` — Dr.GRPO critique says dividing by group std amplifies noise and can cause instability.
2. `loss_agg_mode=token-mean` — Dr.GRPO critique: token-mean weights long responses more, incentivizing longer outputs... Actually the Dr. GRPO paper says token-mean creates a length bias: since the loss is averaged per token over the whole batch, longer sequences contribute more gradient mass. Hmm, actually let me think about this carefully.

Wait — in Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., "Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective"), the critique is:
- Query-level loss normalization (`loss_agg_mode=seq-mean-token-sum` in verl, i.e., dividing by query length) removes length bias.
- Constant-length KL (`low_var_kl`... actually they use no std normalization and constant KL) — the std-based advantage normalization introduces difficulty bias.

In verl's terms:
- `norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo=True` → divides advantage by group std (the original GRPO formulation). Dr. GRPO says this introduces bias: prompts where all responses are wrong (std=0, or all correct) get their advantage inflated... Actually the "difficulty bias": A/(std+ε) amplifies the advantage for groups with small reward differences. When all 8 rollouts score 0 (all wrong, all truncated), std=0 → advantage = 0/(std+ε) → hmm, if all scores equal, mean-centered advantage is 0, then dividing by std gives 0/ε = 0. So no signal. But when 7/8 wrong and 1/8 right, std is small, advantages get amplified hugely. This creates high-variance gradient spikes.

- `loss_agg_mode=token-mean`: gradient mass proportional to token count → long (truncated) responses dominate the gradient. Combined with uniformly negative advantages on all-wrong groups... wait, all-wrong groups have zero advantage under GRPO (mean-centering gives 0 for all). So the truncated responses that score 0 in a group where some other rollout succeeded get negative advantage.

So the loop: hard prompts where the model sometimes succeeds → groups with mixed outcomes → truncated/failed rollouts get A<0, and being 512 tokens long (token-mean) they dominate gradient mass → the model's probability mass on long chain-of-thought gets pushed down broadly → distribution flattens (probability mass spread over many tokens; the "reasoning backbone" tokens lose confidence) → sampling becomes meandering → more truncation → more truncated sequences with A<0 → loop.

Also `clip_ratio_higher` (clip-higher) is absent: DAPO's clip-higher (ε_high=0.28) allows low-probability tokens to increase probability, which counters entropy collapse. But here we see entropy *explosion*, not collapse. Hmm. The direction here is entropy going UP. So the canonical DAPO fixes that matter here are: (a) overlong buffer penalty (soft punishment for exceeding 512-η tokens instead of score-0 truncation) — disabled here; (b) dynamic sampling (filter out all-0 and all-1 groups, oversample) — not enabled (rollout.n fixed, no dynamic sampling config); (c) token-level loss normalization... hmm.

Actually wait — is the entropy explosion caused by token-mean + truncation? Let me reconsider. In DAPO's paper, the "overlong reward shaping" addresses exactly this: truncated responses get 0 reward, which is treated as a negative signal for hard-but-actually-solvable content, degrading performance. And "token-level policy gradient loss" (token-mean over batch) is actually DAPO's choice vs. sample-level. Hmm, DAPO uses token-level loss: "we adopt token-level policy gradient loss" — dividing total loss by total tokens. In verl that's `token-mean`. But DAPO also uses clip-higher to encourage exploration of low-prob tokens, which prevents entropy collapse. And the entropy explosion we see is the opposite problem.

Let me think about what drives entropy UP here:

1. **No entropy bonus needed** — entropy rises as a side effect of negative advantages on long sequences. When you push down the probability of 512-token sequences (all their tokens get negative advantage), the freed probability mass redistributes. The most likely continuation tokens in reasoning (e.g., digits, operators, "The", "so") get systematically suppressed across the whole batch, flattening the conditional distributions. This is the classic "entropy explosion from uniform negative pressure on long sequences" phenomenon. With PPO clip and multiple optimizer steps... hmm, ppo_epochs=1 but 32 mini-batches? Each mini-batch gets 1 gradient step, so each sample is used once. OK.

2. **Std normalization** (`norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo=True`): for GSM8K with binary rewards, groups where 1/8 succeed have std ≈ 0.35, advantages ≈ ±0.94 for the single success/failures... Actually for k=8 with 1 success: mean=0.125, successful gets A=(1-0.125)/std where std=sqrt(0.125*0.875)=0.33 → A≈+2.6; failures get A≈-0.38. The lone success gets hugely amplified positive advantage → its tokens get pushed up hard (clipped at ratio 1.2/0.8 though). Meanwhile the 7 failures share the negative pressure. With clip 0.2 symmetric, the lone success clips quickly; the negative side can go to ratio 0.8 before clipping. Hmm.

3. **KL anchor too weak**: kl_loss_coef=0.001 with low_var_kl. As the policy drifts, kl_loss rose to 0.4-0.5, meaning the coefficient*KL term = 0.0005 — negligible gradient. So no effective anchor → drift continues.

4. **temperature=1.0 with top_p=0.5 during rollout**: rollout entropy measured... the actor entropy is computed on actor logits (full softmax). As the conditional distributions flatten, at temp 1.0 top_p=0.5 nucleus widens, sampling gets more random.

But hold on — the task says "Do not assume that an unusual setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed behavior." So I need to be careful about which settings I name as root causes and make sure each is connected to observed behavior. The strongest, most defensible causal chain:

**Observed:** entropy explosion (0.26→5.06), truncation rate rising in lockstep (0.04→0.37), rollout_log_ppl rising (self-samples become improbable), held-out accuracy flat/falling after step 10, kl_loss rising, training reward plateau ~0.58.

**Root causes (config-level, each connected to evidence):**

A. **Truncated responses receive the full negative outcome signal** (overlong_buffer explicitly disabled via `+reward.reward_kwargs.overlong_buffer_cfg.enable=False`, max_resp_len=512). Evidence: clip_ratio rises with entropy; truncated rollouts in rollouts/*.jsonl score 0 and never contain "####". In GRPO, within a mixed group the truncated response gets A<0 across all 512 tokens. This is the DAPO "overlong penalty shaping" problem in reverse: the model is punished for attempting long reasoning on hard problems, but the punishment (score 0 vs group mean) is applied per-token over the longest sequences.

B. **Token-level loss aggregation** (`loss_agg_mode=token-mean`) — makes gradient mass proportional to sequence length, so those 512-token truncated responses dominate the batch gradient: 30% of sequences carrying ~2-3× the tokens contribute the majority of the loss mass.

C. **Std-normalized advantages** (`norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo=True`) — amplifies advantage in near-uniform groups, creating high-variance updates that keep kicking the policy off its solution manifold (entropy up, kl_loss up, rollout_log_ppl up).

D. **No effective exploration/entropy control**: `entropy_coeff=0` (no regularization either way), no clip-higher, KL anchor 0.001 too weak (kl_loss ~0.4-0.5 → contribution ~4-5e-4 vs. policy loss magnitude). Nothing counteracts the flattening.

E. **top_p=0.5 + temperature=1.0 rollouts**: masks the damage (keeps text coherent) but also interacts: as entropy flattens the full-vocab distribution, the nucleus at p=0.5 grows, exposing sampling to more diffuse continuations → meandering → truncation. Actually wait, is top_p=0.5 causal or just masking? Hmm. The task warns against calling unusual settings causal without connecting to observed behavior. top_p=0.5 is unusual (default 1.0). 300	            shape is (bs, response_length)

302	            shape is (bs, response_length)

306	    id2score = defaultdict(list)
307	    id2mean = {}
308	    id2std = {}

312	        for i in range(bsz):

# NOTE(sgm): this implementation only consider outcome supervision, where the reward is a scalar.
@register_adv_est(AdvantageEstimator.GRPO)  # or simply: @register_adv_est("grpo")
def compute_grpo_outcome_advantage(
    token_level_rewards: torch.Tensor,
    response_mask: torch.Tensor,
    index: np.ndarray,
    epsilon: float = 1e-6,
    norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo: bool = True,
    config: Optional[AlgoConfig] = None,
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    """
    Compute advantage for GRPO, operating only on Outcome reward
    (with only one scalar reward for each response).

    Args:
        token_level_rewards: `(torch.Tensor)`
            shape is (bs, response_length)
        response_mask: `(torch.Tensor)`
            shape is (bs, response_length)
        index: `(np.ndarray)`
            index array for grouping
        epsilon: `(float)`
            small value to avoid division by zero
        norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo: `(bool)`
            whether to scale the GRPO advantage
        config: `(Optional[AlgoConfig])`
            algorithm configuration object

    Note:
        If norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo is True, the advantage is scaled by the std, as in the original GRPO.
        If False, the advantage is not scaled, as in Dr.GRPO (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783).

    Returns:
        advantages: `(torch.Tensor)`
            shape is (bs, response_length)
        Returns: `(torch.Tensor)`
            shape is (bs, response_length)
    """
    scores = token_level_rewards.sum(dim=-1)

    id2score = defaultdict(list)
    id2mean = {}
    id2std = {}

    with torch.no_grad():
        bsz = scores.shape[0]
        for i in range(bsz):
            id2score[index[i]].append(scores[i])
        for idx in id2score:
            if len(id2score[idx]) == 1:
                id2mean[idx] = torch.tensor(0.0)
                id2std[idx] = torch.tensor(1.0)
            elif len(id2score[idx]) > 1:
                scores_tensor = torch.stack(id2score[idx])
                id2mean[idx] = torch.mean(scores_tensor)
                id2std[idx] = torch.std(scores_tensor)
            else:
                raise ValueError(f"no score in prompt index: {idx}")
        for i in range(bsz):
            if norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo:
                scores[i] = (scores[i] - id2mean[index[i]]) / (id2std[index[i]] + epsilon)
            else:
                scores[i] = scores[i] - id2mean[index[i]]
        scores = scores.unsqueeze(-1) * response_mask

    return scores, scores

The GRPO advantage computation is confirmed: mean-centering + std division over 8-sample groups. For a group where 1 of 8 succeeds: mean=0.125, std≈0.354, so success adv ≈ (1−0.125)/0.354 ≈ +2.47, failures ≈ −0.354. For a group where most succeed, failures get large negative: e.g., 7/8 succeed → mean=0.750, std≈0.463 → success adv≈+0.54, single failure ≈ −1.62. So truncated zero-scoring responses carry the largest negative advantage precisely in groups where other rollouts succeed — those long, 512-token truncated responses get -1.62 advantage on every token, and with token-mean aggregation, 512 tokens of that sequence dominate the gradient.

The base model occasionally (0.2-0.5% of rollouts) emits a correct "####" — std normalization amplifies that lone success to +2.475 (vs +0.875 without std normalization), driving fast format acquisition. By step 7, train score is already 0.53.
- Step 10: train score 0.624, val 0.5004 — format acquisition essentially complete. THE PEAK of held-out performance is step 10.
- From step ~13 on: score plateaus ~0.58-0.63 (max 0.666 at step 83), but grad_norm doubles/triples (0.5→3.7), entropy climbs (0.36→5.06 at step 63), truncation climbs 4%→37%, rollout_log_ppl 0.03→2.8. The advantage extremes stay pinned at ±2.475 throughout — the max-magnitude negative advantage is always available from lone-failure groups (or lone successes), i.e., the update keeps slamming ±2.475 on individual sequences.

Also note: `critic/advantages/min = -2.475` persistently — the largest negative advantage always comes from the 7-of-8-success group (single failure, adv=-2.475). Those single failures in otherwise-solved groups — likely the longest, truncated, meandering samples — get the maximal per-token negative pressure. And 512-token sequences vs ~200-token successes → ~2.5× per-sequence gradient mass under token-mean. That's the engine of the entropy explosion.

And the val evidence: val peak at step 10 = 0.5004; final 0.4860; and at step 100 greedy decoding still loses 8.9% of val items to the 512-cap (110/1319 no "####" → score 0), plus 41%... wait no — val score==0 is 51.4% (wrong answers + truncated). The 8.9% cap-truncation alone accounts for a big chunk. If entropy-driven rambling truncation costs ~9% of the val set at greedy, that's the direct held-out damage.

Also important: the "format acquisition" at step 1-10 lifted val from 0.0008 to 0.50. The rest of the run (90 steps, ~360 optimizer steps) added nothing on held-out: 0.50 → 0.486 (slightly negative). Training score rose 0.62→0.67 max — pure training-side overfitting/entropy churn.

Now — one more mechanism link to verify quickly: is it really the TRUNCATED sequences that get the -2.475? From the group analysis at step 100: 19 mixed groups with 25 bad members (18.8% of 133... wait 19 mixed groups × 8 = 152 rows, 25 bad members). from transformers import AutoTokenizer
import json, math
from collections import defaultdict
tok=AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('models/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct')
for stepf in ['50','100']:
    rows=[json.loads(l) for l in open(f'results/run100/rollouts/{stepf}.jsonl')]
    for r in rows: r['ntok']=len(tok(r['output'])['input_ids'])
    groups=defaultdict(list)
    for r in rows: groups[r['input']].append(r)
    T=sum(r['ntok'] for r in rows)
    # batch-wide token mass by outcome
    zero_tok=sum(r['ntok'] for r in rows if r['score']==0)
    zero_trunc_tok=sum(r['ntok'] for r in rows if r['score']==0 and r['ntok']>=512)
    # mixed groups: recompute exact GRPO advantages
    import statistics
    pos_mag=0; neg_mag=0; neg_tok=0; pos_tok=0; tot_tok_mixed=0
    trunc_bad=[]; advs=[]
    for inp,g in groups.items():
        sc=[x['score'] for x in g]
        if 0 < sum(sc) < len(sc):
            m=sum(sc)/len(sc); s=statistics.stdev(sc)+1e-6
            for x in g:
                a=(x['score']-m)/s
                advs.append((a,x['ntok'],x['score']==0,x['ntok']>=512))
                tot_tok_mixed+=x['ntok']
                if a<0:
                    neg_mag+=abs(a)*x['ntok']; neg_tok+=x['ntok']
                    if x['ntok']>=512: trunc_bad.append((a,x['ntok']))
                else: pos_mag+=a*x['ntok']; pos_tok+=x['ntok']
    negtot=sum(a*t for a,t,_,_ in advs if a<0); postot=sum(a*t for a,t,_,_ in advs if a>0)
    print(f"step {stepf}: batch response tokens={T}; zero-score rows carry {zero_tok/T:.1%} of token mass, of which >=512-cap {zero_trunc_tok/T:.1%}")
    mm=[x for x in advs]
    mixed_T=sum(t for _,t,_,_ in mm)
    print(f"   mixed groups: {sum(1 for inp,g in groups.items() if 0<sum(x['score'] for x in g)<len(g))} groups; their token mass={mixed_T/T:.1%} of batch")
    print(f"   within mixed groups: negative-adv token mass={neg_tok/mixed_T:.1%}, |A|*tok negative={negtot:.0f} vs positive={postot:.0f} (ratio {abs(negtot)/max(postot,1e-9):.2f})")
    tb=[a for a,t in trunc_bad]
    print(f"   truncated(512-cap) zero-score members in mixed groups: {len(tb)}, advs={sorted(set(round(a,2) for a in tb))}")
    # mean length of success vs failure in mixed groups
    ok=[t for a,t,z,tr in mm if not z]; bad=[t for a,t,z,tr in mm if z]
    print(f"   mean len success={sum(ok)/len(ok):.0f} tok vs failure={sum(bad)/len(bad):.0f} tok in mixed groups")
EOF

steps.reasoning_content:
Excellent, decisive numbers at step 100:
- Zero-score rows carry 56.6% of the batch's response-token mass (they are longer: 348 tok mean vs 228 for successes).
- Inside mixed groups, token-weighted negative advantage mass exceeds positive by ~1.53× (21848 vs 14239).
- Truncated members in mixed groups get advantages as strong as −2.47 and −1.62 — the largest negative magnitudes in the whole batch — and they are the longest sequences, so under `loss_agg_mode=token-mean` each of their 512 tokens carries that full negative advantage. This is the asymmetry: positive advantage is spread over short sequences, negative advantage concentrated over long ones.

That is the core mechanism. Under token-mean, the gradient per token = advantage × ∇log π(token). The batch gradient is dominated by 512 tokens × (−1.6 to −2.47) from truncated sequences, plus all the other zero-score-but-under-512 failures (they also get negative advantage in mixed groups and are longer on average). The net effect is a broad push-down on exactly the token patterns that appear in long meandering CoT: connectives, numbers, "The", "So", etc. — the model's confident next-token logits flatten, entropy rises 0.26→5.06, and at temperature 1.0 + top_p=0.5 the sampled continuations become more diffuse → longer, more meandering → more truncation → more of the batch becomes long negative-advantage mass → self-reinforcing loop. corr(entropy, clip_ratio)=0.909 over 100 steps.

And the KL anchor is too weak to stop it: kl_loss reached 0.52 but kl_loss_coef=0.001 → KL term ≈ 5e-4 vs pg_loss ≈ 0.01-0.04 (1-2 orders of magnitude smaller), so it barely restrains drift. entropy_coeff=0 means no entropy shaping at all. No clip-higher. Overlong buffer explicitly disabled — so truncated sequences are treated as plain failures with the harshest negative advantage (up to −2.47), rather than receiving a shaped penalty or being filtered out (no dynamic sampling).

Now, what about the "all-fail" groups? Note GRPO gives A=0 to all-fail and all-success groups, so those contribute nothing (only groups with 0 < successes < 8). At step 100: 19/128 groups are mixed and carry 16.4% of token mass. That's where all learning signal comes from. Also worth noting: with std-normalization, the amplified ±2.475 (1-of-8 groups) yields the largest single-sequence gradient contributions: a lone 512-token truncated sequence at −2.475 × 512 tokens is a colossal per-token pushdown.

Hmm wait — one more consideration. Let me double-check the direction claim "pushing down probability of long sequences flattens the distribution / raises entropy". Is there an alternative reading: the entropy rise is a healthy exploration increase? The standard DAPO paper narrative is entropy collapse; but entropy *explosion* is also documented (e.g., in "The Entropy Mechanism of RL for LLMs" and DAPO's clip-higher discussion mentions entropy fluctuating; several papers note both collapse and explosion as two failure modes of unstable training). The evidence that this is pathological rather than healthy exploration:
1. Held-out accuracy didn't improve — after the step-10 format gain (0.50), it *declined* to 0.43 by step 40 and hovered 0.43-0.50 for the rest, never exceeding step 10's 0.50 despite 90 more steps of training.
2. rollout_log_ppl 0.033→2.8: the policy assigns e^-2.8 ≈ 6% probability to its own sampled tokens — the model has drifted into a region where its own samples are improbable under itself. That's off-policy-like drift within on-policy training, a signature of policy overshoot/unstability, not healthy exploration.
3. Training score dropped from 0.63 (step 10) to ~0.46-0.49 at steps 16-17 and 63 — i.e., training reward itself degraded as entropy spiked; it recovered partially (0.58-0.67 band) but with high volatility.
4. clip_ratio (truncation) rose in lockstep — 37% of rollouts truncated at the joint peak. Truncated = automatic zero score. So the flattening directly destroys reward: the entropy spike trades answer-completion for meandering.

The entropy spike and the score dip coincide exactly at steps 16-17 and 63. And val at step 20 = 0.475, step 30 = 0.446, step 40 = 0.430 — the val degradation tracks the entropy explosion with a lag. That's a solid causal narrative.

One more check to nail "meandering": are the truncated step-100 rollouts actually rambling/diffuse rather than doing useful long reasoning? From the earlier session I looked at examples; let me look at 2-3 truncated outputs at step 100 to characterize (e.g., repetitive loops or incoherent drift). And check val truncated ones too. Also confirm the earlier finding that non-truncated text remains locally coherent (top_p masking).

Also — the red herring (rollout_corr artifacts). Let me verify the claim about vLLM renormalized log probs once more by checking the actual correlation direction and the sign story: kl = E[log π_rollout − log π_train] = +0.185 (rollout more confident), ppl_ratio = exp? Let me recall definitions: rollout_log_ppl = mean NLL under rollout log probs = 0.033 at step 1? Wait: rollout_log_ppl at step 1 = 0.033, at 63 = 2.816. And ppl_ratio = rollout_ppl/training_ppl? Let me get the exact definitions from rollout_corr_helper.py to state them correctly in the report. From the summary: `kl = E[log π_rollout − log π_train]` "positive means rollout policy more confident than training policy"; ppl_ratio ≈ 1.13; chi2_token = E[ρ²]−1 ≈ −0.21 which is mathematically impossible for true χ² (E[ρ²]−1 ≥ 0 by Jensen, since E[ρ]=... well E[ρ²]≥E[ρ]² and E[ρ]≈1). And kl = E[log π_rollout − log π_train] > 0 → same story. ppl_ratio = training_ppl/rollout_ppl or rollout_ppl/training_ppl? = 1.13 — need the exact def. Let me grep quickly.

Hmm, actually if vLLM renormalizes after top_p, probs would differ systematically (diff mean 0.018 is small in absolute terms but could be systematic: vLLM probs higher by ~0.02 mean). Actually — pearson correlation 0.986 between the two prob vectors is high; the systematic offset is the renormalization. But there's a subtlety: does verl's debug metric show this because of renormalization, or because weights are synced? At step 1 pearson was 0.71 (base model, pre-sync?) rising to 0.99. Anyway — the key point stands: weight sync is fine (the actor recomputes old_log_probs from its own full softmax, which is what the PPO ratio uses; the vLLM log probs are only used in diagnostics), and the rollout_corr artifacts are top_p-renormalization artifacts, not off-policy training. Let me verify the exact definitions to write this precisely.

Actually, one thing I should double check: is it *actually true* that vLLM renormalizes log probs when top_p < 1? In vLLM, `logprobs` returned are computed from the sampled-token distribution. vLLM's sampler applies top_p/top_k by masking logits and then sampling from softmax(masked logits) — the returned logprob for the sampled token is log softmax over the *filtered* distribution. Yes, this is a known behavior: vLLM logprobs under top_k/top_p sampling are post-filter renormalized. In newer vLLM versions, there's a config `calculate_log_probs` or they renormalize... The observed metrics (systematically positive kl and ppl_ratio ≈ 1.1, impossible negative chi2) are consistent with this. Also the helper file itself may document that top_p causes this. Also check: verl has an option `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.log_prob_recompute_or_load`... not needed.

Doesn't matter much: the conclusion is weight sync is healthy (diff_mean 0.018, pearson 0.99), and the residual systematic difference is the top_p renormalization signature. Both supported.

So `ppl_ratio_i = rollout_ppl? no: ppl_ratio = exp(mean_log_prob_rollout - mean_log_prob_training) per sequence = training_ppl/rollout_ppl... wait:

log_ppl_diff = mean_log_prob_rollout − mean_log_prob_training. PPL = exp(−mean_log_prob). So exp(log_ppl_diff) = exp(−mean_log_prob_training)/exp(−mean_log_prob_rollout) = training_ppl/rollout_ppl. ppl_ratio = mean over sequences of training_ppl_i/rollout_ppl_i. Observed 1.13: training PPL is 13% higher than rollout PPL → the actor (training policy, full softmax) assigns *lower* likelihood to the sampled tokens than vLLM's post-top_p-renormalized distribution does. Consistent with vLLM renormalizing over the nucleus: restricted-and-renormalized probs > full-softmax probs.

And `rho` = π_training/π_rollout (IS weight), chi2_token = E[ρ²]−1 ≥ 0 in expectation for a consistent estimator; observed −0.21 is impossible unless the two "distributions" aren't consistent (which is exactly the case when one is a renormalized restriction of the other). So the artifacts are explained. The kl = E[log π_rollout − log π_train] > 0 likewise.

I verified `apply_bypass_mode` exists — correction disabled because rollout_correction config unset; the actor recomputes old_log_probs from full-softmax logits (timing_s/old_log_prob present in metrics: recomputation happens). Now let me look at 2 truncated outputs at step 100 to characterize "meandering" and confirm text remains locally coherent (top_p masking claim), then check the val outputs of step-0 for the \boxed claim (already established pre-compaction: 650/1319 \boxed, 28/1319 ####). And also verify sample outputs at step 100 for degenerate repetition (should be none — pre-compaction established).

Then write the deliverable.

Actually, let me also double-check one potential alternative root cause to be fair: **is the entropy explosion caused by std-normalization (norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo=True) or by token-mean + truncation-negative-pressure?** Both are config choices. Evidence to discriminate:

- The advantage extremes ±2.475 appear already at step 2-4 — during the healthy bootstrap phase, and entropy stayed low (0.26-0.37) through step 10-12 while score climbed to 0.63. So std-amplified advantages alone didn't cause flattening; they drove fast format learning *successfully*.
- Entropy took off at steps 13-17 (0.62→2.25) exactly when clip_ratio jumped 0.04→0.31 and score dropped 0.63→0.49. So the explosion coincides with the rise of the truncated-long-negative-advantage mass, not merely with amplified advantages.

Actually wait — let me reconsider. Is the direction of causality maybe: entropy rises → more meandering → truncation? Which is cause and which effect? The loop is self-reinforcing; the *initiator* is what matters. What initiated entropy rise at step ~13?

Consider: as the model learns to answer with "####" format quickly (score 0.63 at step 10), what happens on harder problems? It must produce longer reasoning to reach the answer. For hard problems, groups become mixed (1-2 of 8 succeed). The failures there are long (352 vs 232 tokens average). Two candidate initiators:
(a) token-mean weighting of negative-adv long sequences (the length bias — Dr.GRPO critique #1: token-level normalization "trivially fits a length bias"); 
(b) std-normalization amplification.

Note the literature: Dr. GRPO paper identifies "query-level loss normalization" as the fix for a *length bias*; the paper "Unbiased on-chain... " no. Let me think about what token-mean does mathematically: gradient = Σ_tokens A_t ∇log π_t / Σ_tokens 1. A truncated 512-token sequence with A=−2.475 contributes −2.475×512 units of "push-down" on its tokens, while a 100-token success with A=+0.35 contributes +35 units of "push-up". Net: overwhelmingly negative pressure on long-form CoT token patterns. Meanwhile within the successful short sequences, the positive pressure concentrates on the narrow "#### N" answer patterns. The result: the broad "reasoning body" tokens (which are shared across many contexts) get suppressed, while format tokens get reinforced. This flattens conditional distributions on all the suppressed contexts → entropy up on the "body" tokens; and because sampling at temp 1.0 from flatter distributions yields more branching → longer responses → more truncation. That's exactly the observed joint dynamics, and it's also what the val data shows: format compliance improved to 88% (#### present) while accuracy stayed at 0.49 — the model retained the "####" habit (short, well-reinforced) but the reasoning quality degraded (broad suppression), plus 8-11% of val answers truncated (automatic 0).

Also note val score 0 at step 0 = 99.9% wrong (format missing: only 2.1% had ####, 5.3% truncated-and-no-####, rest probably \boxed or no marker). By step 50/100, #### present 87.6-88.2%, truncation 8.9-13%, score 0 = 51-54%. So of the 0-val-score rows at step 100: 110 truncated (8.3% of all rows) and 568 wrong-but-formatted (43%). The trained model is *worse* on held-out accuracy than... well, it's better than base (which scored 0.08% due to format) but the actual reasoning capability didn't improve after step 10.
